chapter_theme: Kuruntokai 161 to 180: short speeches across all five lands. A hill man stands in the night rain at a wakeful house; the jasmine laughs at a lonely man in the rains; a girl hears her own sleeplessness in the sea; a courtesan swears by the sea that she has no claim; a man rides the palmyra horse; a young wife cooks for her husband's one word of praise; a wife curses her own laughing teeth; and in the wasteland poems the woman and her friend weigh wealth against grace and ask whether the absent man has hardened.

161.reading: On a night when daylight has gone dark, the rain will not stop and a wind blows that would chill even a ghoul's eyes, while her mother clutches the boys with tiger-tooth pendants and cries out in alarm, the girl wonders what could have possessed the hill man, his chest smelling of sandal, to come and stand outside like an elephant in the rain.
161.nuance: The danger is doubled: the storm outside and the wakeful mother inside. The elephant standing silent and soaked in the rain gives his bulk and his patience at once; the cry அன்னா is the household's alarm, which the girl must hear while knowing who is out there.

thinai_evidence.note: the hill man, the tiger-tooth pendants and sandal fix the hills, and the night visit is kalavu

comparisons.tenor: the lover standing outside the house in the night rain, like an elephant standing in the downpour

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the girl speaks of the night visit, most likely to her friend

162.reading: In the wide watered land the rains have nursed, at the dull evening when everyone goes home, the man alone hails the jasmine and asks whether it is fair to put on a smile with its small white buds and seem to laugh at those who are by themselves.
162.nuance: The buds are not called like a smile; they have taken the smile from someone (முறுவல் கொண்டனை), so the flower wears the absent woman's laugh. The evening when many come home is the mullai hour of return, which makes his being away the sharper.

thinai_evidence.note: the rainy season, evening and the jasmine are mullai's time and flower

comparisons.tenor: the jasmine opening its buds, as if laughing at the lonely man
the small white buds as a smile

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: he addresses the jasmine; he is away from home in the rainy season

163.reading: The girl asks the sea who has hurt it, since on the great shore of the grove, where fish-fed herons spread like a flock of the Puzhiyar's small-headed white sheep and the waves toss the white-flowered thazhai, she hears its voice even in the dead of night.
163.nuance: The question is turned outward but answers itself: she hears the sea at midnight only because she is awake, so the sea's unrest is the mirror of her own, and யார் அணங்குற்றனை asks of the sea what others might ask of her.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea shore and a sleepless night of lament are neythal

comparisons.tenor: the white herons spread over the shore, like a flock of the Puzhiyar's small-headed white sheep

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses the sea

164.reading: The man's courtesan tells her friend: may the cool great sea east of the hill town of the ancient Velir, where the vaalai fish and its heavy-bellied young mate snatch the sweet fruit of the clustered mango, strike me, if I am the one the wife sulks over in her simplicity, if I am anything to her husband.
164.nuance: An oath sworn by a named sea is a public statement: the courtesan disowns any claim on the man so that the wife's quarrel falls back on him. The fish pair feeding on fallen mango has been read as a hidden image of the man and his pregnant wife at ease, but it is the oath-place's description, with no second pair to anchor it, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's sulking over the husband and another woman is marutham's quarrel

thurai_akam.speaker: parathai
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her own friend (தோழி, line 4); the oath is meant to reach the wife

165.reading: The man tells his heart that, like drinking toddy on top of being already merry, it has burned on top of its desire, and has given way like a salt cart standing on a steep bank that melts away in a heavy downpour, from seeing her thick dark hair and natural grace.
165.nuance: Both images make the sight a second blow on an earlier one: toddy on top of joy, rain on top of salt. The salt cart is a coast and trade thing brought into a hill poem, and its cargo does not break, it dissolves, which is how he says his resolve went.

thinai_evidence.note: a man undone by the first sight of a girl is the meeting of kurinji

comparisons.tenor: the heart's fresh desire coming on top of its earlier joy, like toddy drunk by one already merry
the heart giving way at the sight of her, like a salt cart that dissolves in a heavy downpour

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the நீ of line 2 is his own heart

166.reading: Where the waves of the cool sea draw back and the white-winged storks move off in a line to feed on ayirai fish, the town of Maranthai is good indeed, says the friend, but for one who stays there all alone it turns to desolation.
166.nuance: The storks move and feed in a row (நிரை), the company the speaker lacks; the praise of the town is granted only to be withdrawn by the last line. ஒருதனி doubles the word for alone.

thinai_evidence.note: the sea's waves, storks and ayirai fish are the shore's things

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; read as the friend telling the man that the woman left alone in his town will suffer; who stays alone is not stated

iraicchi.act: the storks move off together in a line and feed side by side
iraicchi.sense: even the storks of the shore feed in company, so a town, however good, is misery to the one left to live there alone

167.reading: The foster mother reports that the young wife, wiping her soft kanthal-like fingers that had kneaded thick curd on her unwashed garment and with her lily-like kohl eyes filled with seasoning smoke, stirred and cooked the sweet-sour stew herself, and when her husband ate it saying it was sweet, her bright-browed face glowed with a quiet joy.
167.nuance: Every detail of the girl's discomfort (curd on her fingers, a dirty cloth, smoke in her painted eyes) is the price of the one word இனிது, and the joy is small and fine (நுண்ணிதின்). The foster mother, who knew her as a child, notices that she now cooks with her own hands (தான் துழந்து).

thinai_evidence.note: a wife keeping house content with her husband is mullai's karpu

comparisons.tenor: her soft fingers as kanthal flowers
her kohl-lined eyes as blue water lilies

thurai_akam.speaker: sevili
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; by convention the foster mother reports the married daughter's household to the mother

168.reading: The man says she is fragrant and cool, like dripping plump buds of the rain-season pithikam packed together in a fresh palmyra-leaf basket and opened out at dawn after heavy rain, her dark body lovely and her broad curved shoulders like a raft on a flood; for him there is no joining her and leaving her, and to live apart from her is even less possible.
168.nuance: The raft simile is the poem's argument: shoulders that carry one across a flood are not left behind. மணத்தலும் தணத்தலும் இலமே says that with her there is no cycle of union and parting at all, so the journey he weighs is ruled out.

thinai_evidence.note: he weighs leaving her and refuses: the parting is the situation

comparisons.vehicle: மாரிப் பித்திகத்து நீர்வார் கொழுமுகை இரும்பனம் பசுங்குடைப் பலவுடன் பொதிந்து பெரும்பெயல் விடியல் விரித்துவிட் டன்ன
comparisons.tenor: her fragrance and coolness, like rain-season pithikam buds packed in a palm-leaf basket and opened at a wet dawn
her broad shoulders, like a raft on a flood

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; he speaks of her in the third person, refusing a journey

169.reading: The wife tells the man: may the bright white teeth that laughed with you snap off at once like an elephant's tusk struck on a rock on the wasteland road; like the bowl in which bards poured fresh fish, we too reek to ourselves and cannot have you, so may our life break.
169.nuance: புலவு (the stink of fish) carries புலவி (the sulk): she reeks to herself as the bards' fish bowl does. The curse falls on her own teeth, the part of her that once laughed with him, so the anger turns inward.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife's bitter sulk at a husband who is not hers is marutham

comparisons.tenor: her teeth snapping off, like the tusk of an elephant on the wasteland road that strikes a rock
her own reek to herself, like the bowl the bards poured fresh fish into

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses him as ஐய

170.reading: Let many say it, those who do not know, says the girl; I know well that the bond of the man of the hill country, where an elephant seeking a pool gulps a mouthful of the fresh-spiked eruvai grass the waterfall has brought down, will not come to an end.
170.nuance: The elephant takes what the falls bring it without labour, which suits a love she counts as given; but the line that carries her claim, கேண்மை தலைபோகாமை, can be read either as a bond that will not break or one that will not reach its end in marriage, and the poem's confidence rests on that reading.

thinai_evidence.note: the waterfall, the elephant and the hill man are kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; she answers the talk of the many

171.reading: Look now, friend, says the girl: like a great beast caught in a fish net set in the long pond on the bank of the new fierce flood, what will come of the strangers' suit?
171.nuance: A fish net cannot hold a large beast; it tears and the catch is lost. The strangers (நொதுமலர்) who have come asking for her are the net, and the girl who already belongs to another is what they cannot hold, so her question mocks their effort.

thinai_evidence.note: the flood, the pond and the fish net are field and river things

comparisons.tenor: the strangers' marriage suit, like a great beast caught in a fish net that cannot hold it

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her friend (தோழி, line 1) while strangers seek her in marriage

172.reading: In the aching evening when the bat with its soft flapping wings makes for the fruiting tree, the woman asks whether those who left her alone here are happy being alone themselves, while her heart toils without limit like the trodden bellows of a forge one village set up for the common work of seven.
172.nuance: The bellows is worked by everyone and rests for no one, so the heart is pumped by every hour of the evening. Her question imagines him as lonely as she is and stops short of saying he is not.

thinai_evidence.note: the lament at evening, left alone, is neythal's hour and uri

comparisons.vehicle: ஏழூர்ப் பொதுவினைக் கோரூர் யாத்த உலைவாங்கு மிதிதோல் போலத்
comparisons.tenor: her heart toiling without rest, like the trodden bellows of a forge one village keeps for the work of seven

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of those who left her

iraicchi.act: the bat flies at evening to the tree where its fruit is
iraicchi.sense: even the bat goes at dusk to where its food and rest are, yet the man stays away from her

173.reading: The man says that, mounting the palmyra horse hung with a many-stranded garland of fresh gold-like avirai flowers, its bells ringing, casting off shame as the pain within him grows ever worse, he is ready to go there, knowing that this town will stand before her and name her fault, saying 'such a woman did this'.
173.nuance: The madal works through the town's tongue: his shame is to become her blame (அவள் பழி), which is what forces her kin. The garland of avirai is the madal rider's own sign; நாண் அட்டு says shame is killed, not merely set aside.

thinai_evidence.note: riding the palmyra horse with shame cast off is madal, which belongs to perunthinai, not to the hill land the colophon gives

comparisons.tenor: the fresh avirai flowers, golden like gold

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivan
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; the madal threat is conventionally spoken to the girl's friend

174.reading: If he leaves us for wealth, not saying the roads are hard through the lonely wasteland the rain has forsaken, where the dried pod of the forked-thorn cactus bursts with a crack and scatters a pair of soft-feathered doves, then in this world wealth alone is wealth, and grace is something no one has.
174.nuance: The doves are a pair (துணைப் புற) driven apart by a sound, a picture of what his going does, but they do nothing themselves, so they stay scene. The verdict is about the world, not only the man: பொருளே மன்ற பொருளே and அருளே மன்ற ஆருமில் லதுவே are built as a pair, wealth affirmed and grace orphaned.

thinai_evidence.note: parting for wealth across the dry waste is paalai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: the colophon names no addressee; she speaks of him in the third person

175.reading: Of the lord of the wide waters, on whose wave-beaten shore of packed sand swarms of many-winged bees, wanting the season's honey, crowd the dark branches of the wet punnai, the girl tells her friend that she will not go about telling everyone 'I do not grieve; what is wrong here?'; let things be as they will, what is the gossip to her?
175.nuance: The friend's advice to hide her pain is refused: the pretence that would quiet the town is what she will not perform. The construction of lines 5 and 6 is loose, and whether she refuses or grants the friend's request turns on how கூறல் is taken.

thinai_evidence.note: the wave-beaten shore, the punnai and the lord of the coast are neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her friend (தோழி, line 5)

176.reading: The friend says: he did not come for one day or two, but came for many days, spoke humble words and softened my good heart, and then went off like honey ripe on the high cliff; where is he now, he who was our support, while my heart runs muddy like thundering rain poured out on another land?
176.nuance: The friend speaks of her own heart because the lover first won the go-between: his humble words were addressed to her, so his absence is her betrayal too. The rain falls on another country, wasted where it is not needed, and so her heart's flood reaches no one.

thinai_evidence.note: the cliff honey is a hill thing, and the lover is the one courted in kalavu

comparisons.tenor: the lover gone beyond reach, like honey ripened high on a cliff

comparisons.vehicle: வேறுபுல னன்னாட்டுப் பெய்த ஏறுடை மழையிற் கலிழும்
comparisons.tenor: her heart running muddy, like thundering rain poured out on another land

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she speaks of her own heart and asks where he is

177.reading: The sea's roar has died down, the shore grove has dimmed, the dark backwater of the ford looks forlorn, and the anril that lives on the fronds of the palmyra in the common ground calls softly; will he come today, friend, the man who, afraid even of parting when we sulked, pressed on us a love hard to leave?
177.nuance: The stilled sea, the dim grove and the hushed anril are all evening's quiet, and the friend sets against them the man's old fear of any parting. Line 5's reading differs between editions (நாந்தப், நாம் நகப், நாம் தம்), and whether the sulk was theirs or his changes the last two lines.

thinai_evidence.note: the stilled sea, shore grove and backwater at dusk are neythal

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses her friend the heroine (வாழி தோழி, line 5)

178.reading: The friend tells the man: like those who pluck the hollow-stemmed water lily in the cool field where ayirai fish spread and yet thirst for water, you once trembled lying between her breasts; now that we have become as hard to see as the crescent moon one worships, you have borne a great deal, and I grieve for it.
178.nuance: The irony is in the reversal: he who shook at the gap between two breasts now endures a long absence with ease. The lily-pickers stand in water and thirst, which was his old love: desire even in possession. நோகோ யானே pities him only in form.

thinai_evidence.note: the cool field and the lily-pickers are marutham's, and the barb at a neglecting husband is its quarrel

comparisons.tenor: his old trembling even when lying close to her, like lily-pickers who stand in water and still thirst
the women now rarely seen by him, like the crescent moon that one sees only to worship

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses him (நீர், நுமக்கு)

179.reading: The friend tells the hunter: you have chased the wild beast through the noisy forest, the day has darkened and your dogs are worn out; do not go, sir; that is our village, there in the curve of the high hill among the stunted bamboo that a foolish soft-mouthed elephant chewed after eating green clustered bamboo that had torn the sweet honeycomb.
179.nuance: The invitation to stay is given as plain hospitality, a tired man and tired dogs at nightfall, and the village is placed by a landmark only a local would use. The young elephant tasting honey-smeared bamboo has been read as a hidden image of the sweetness waiting there, but no situation in the poem anchors it, so it stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the hunt, the dogs, the hill slope and the elephant are kurinji

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: she addresses him as ஐஇய

180.reading: The friend wonders whether the man has reached his wealth, having crossed the waste where, when the herd of great broad-footed tuskers comes, with nails thick like a demon's teeth, the lone pining bamboo, like a sugarcane joint that has died and fallen on the rock, stands tall; and whether those who left, letting the lovely lines of her waist fade, have grown hard of heart in the land they went to.
180.nuance: The lone bamboo is the waste's emblem of what survives alone, worn like a dead cane joint; the friend's two questions move from the road (did he arrive?) to his heart (has it hardened?), and the second is the one she fears.

thinai_evidence.note: a man gone across the waste for wealth is paalai's parting

comparisons.tenor: the elephants' thick nails, like a demon's teeth
the lone wasted bamboo, like the joint of a sugarcane that has died and lies on the rock

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: no addressee is named; she wonders aloud about the absent man, with the heroine in mind

links.note: Kural 1090 says liquor delights only one who drinks it while love delights at a look; in Kuruntokai 165 the man, having only seen her hair and grace, says the sight came on his desire like toddy on top of joy.
links.teaches: The poem accepts the Kural's claim that love works by sight alone but denies the contrast with liquor: for the man who has looked, seeing acts exactly like a second drink, so the couplet's rule holds while its comparison is turned around.

links.note: In Kural 1133 the man says he once had shame and manliness and now has the palmyra horse; in Kuruntokai 173 he mounts it with shame killed (நாணட்டு) and says the town will name her fault.
links.teaches: The Kural counts only what the madal costs the rider, his shame; the poem names what it is for, turning his public shame into her blame on the town's tongue, which is the pressure that makes the threat work on her kin.

links.note: In Kural 1222 the woman asks the pale evening whether its partner is as hard as hers; in Kuruntokai 163 she asks the sea who has hurt it, since she hears it crying at midnight.
links.teaches: Both women treat a natural thing as a fellow sufferer, but the poem shows how the projection is built: she knows the sea grieves because she herself is awake to hear it, so the sympathy is evidence of her sleeplessness rather than a fancy.

links.note: Kural 247 says this world is not for those without wealth and the other world not for those without grace; Kuruntokai 174 says that if he leaves for wealth, in this world wealth alone is wealth and grace has no one.
links.teaches: The heroine grants the Kural's premise about this world in its own words (இவ்வுலகத்து) and drops its consolation: with no other world in view, the couplet's balance of wealth and grace collapses into a world where grace has no owner.

links.note: In Akananuru 75 the man quotes the saying that effort, not grace, is a man's wealth and declines to follow it; in Kuruntokai 174 the woman, whose man did follow it, concludes that wealth alone is wealth and grace belongs to no one.
links.teaches: Together they show the wealth-over-grace maxim as a live argument of the paalai poems argued from both ends: the man can refuse it out of love, and the woman, when he does not, turns it from a rule of conduct into a bitter verdict on the whole world.

links.note: In Kural 1148 the woman says hoping to quench love with gossip is like quenching fire with ghee; in Kuruntokai 175 she refuses to tell everyone she is not grieving and asks what the gossip matters.
links.teaches: The Kural's woman answers the town with an argument that talk only feeds love, while the poem's woman refuses the remedy the friend proposes, public denial, so the pair separates two defences against gossip: rebutting its power and declining to perform the concealment that would silence it.

links.note: Naladiyar 363 calls a wife who does not enter the kitchen at dawn a disease and one who does not serve what she cooked a demon; Kuruntokai 167 shows a young wife, smoke in her kohl eyes, cooking and serving with delight at her husband's praise. On the Naladiyar's reading the act is a duty enforced by threat; on the poem's it is the wife's own joy.
links.teaches: The same kitchen duty that the ethics book defines by the horror of its failure is shown in the Sangam poem as freely chosen pleasure, so the pair shows the domestic norm seen from the husband's fear and from the wife's satisfaction.

links.note: Both poems are by Kachchippettu Nannakaiyar and both ask about the man who left (துறந்தோர்): in 172 the woman at evening asks whether he is happy being alone; in 180 the friend asks whether he has grown hard in the land he went to.
links.teaches: Read together, the poet's two questions mark the turn of a long absence: the first still imagines him as lonely as she is, the second fears his heart has changed, so the doubt moves from his comfort to his constancy.

source_issues: 176: line 1 (ஒருநாள் வாரலன் இருநாள் வாரலன்) is not in sangamtamil.com's text; line 5 (ஆசா கெந்தை யாண்டுளன் கொல்லோ) repeats as Kuruntokai 325 line 4, and its first words are hard to divide.
177: line 5 varies (ours நாந்தப், tamilvu.org நாம் நகப், sangamtamil.com நாம் தம்); the sense of the closing lines depends on it.
173: the colophon thinai is குறிஞ்சி, but the poem is a madal speech, which the Tholkappiyam places under perunthinai; the disagreement is recorded in thinai.

180: the poet's name, printed at the end of the verse in the source, was moved to the poet field (per the text flag); lines 1 to 4 are a dense description whose construction (what the herd does to the bamboo) is not certain.
170: line 5 கேண்மை தலைபோகாமை can be read as a bond that will not end or one that will not reach completion; the reading taken is the first.
